nameStory: Mock strawberry gets its name because it's a clever imposter – it looks almost exactly like a wild strawberry plant with its three-leaflet leaves and small red berries. The word 'mock' means to imitate or copy, which is exactly what this little plant does so well that it fools people into thinking they've found wild strawberries!
description: Mock strawberry is a low-growing, creeping plant that spreads along the ground with trailing stems called runners. It produces small white flowers that turn into bright red berries that look remarkably like tiny strawberries. The plant stays close to the ground, rarely getting taller than a few inches, but can spread widely to form patches. Its leaves are divided into three leaflets, just like true strawberry plants.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with 5 petals that feel papery when touched – this is the dead giveaway that separates it from true strawberries, which have white flowers

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small red berries that look like strawberries but are hard and tasteless, with seeds sitting on top of the surface rather than embedded within

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves (called trifoliate) that are soft to touch with visible veins and toothed edges, growing alternately along the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeping plant that spreads by runners along the ground, forming low mats that rarely rise above 4 inches tall

habitat: Mock strawberry thrives in disturbed areas like lawn edges, garden borders, and woodland clearings throughout New England. It prefers moist, partially shaded spots with rich soil but is quite adaptable and can grow in full sun to deep shade. You'll often find it creeping around the bases of trees, along pathways, and in areas where the soil has been disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Yellow flowers begin appearing in late spring, standing out brightly against the fresh green three-part leaves that emerge as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming and fruiting season, when you'll see yellow flowers and red berries on the same plant simultaneously throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn reddish or remain green well into fall, with some late berries still visible before the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground in harsh winters but may remain semi-evergreen in protected spots or during mild winters.

funFact: Mock strawberry is actually a master of deception from the rose family – it evolved to look exactly like edible wild strawberries to trick animals into eating and dispersing its seeds, even though its berries are completely flavorless and somewhat dry!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with wild strawberry (Fragaria species), but remember this simple trick: yellow flowers mean mock, white flowers mean yummy! The berries also give it away – mock strawberry fruits are hard and flavorless, while true wild strawberries are soft, sweet, and juicy.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is native to Asia but has naturalized so well in North America that many people assume it's native. Some botanists still call it by its old scientific name Duchesnea indica, so you might see both names in field guides.
compareHints: Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries. Most other cinquefoils also have yellow flowers, but their leaves and growth habits are quite different – they tend to be more upright rather than creeping, and their leaves are palmately divided into five leaflets rather than three.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
